The '''Asia Society''' is a [[501(c)(3) organization]] that focuses on educating the world about [[Asia]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Roberts |first4=Andrea |last4=Suozzo |first2=Alec |last2=Glassford |first3=Ash |last3=Ngu |first1=Brandon |date=2013-05-09 |title=Asia Society - Nonprofit Explorer |url=https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/133234632 |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=ProPublica |language=en |archive-date=May 25, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240525162341/https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/133234632 |url-status=live }}</ref> It has several centers in the United States (Manhattan, Washington, D.C., Houston, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Seattle) and around the world (Hong Kong, Manila, Seoul, Melbourne, Sydney, Tokyo,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Society |first=Asia |date=March 30, 2018 |title=Asia Society to Open Center in Japan |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/asia-society-to-open-center-in-japan-300622078.html |access-date=November 26, 2024 |work=PR Newswire |pages=1 |archive-date=December 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203120113/https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/asia-society-to-open-center-in-japan-300622078.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Mumbai, Delhi,<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 3, 2022 |title=Asia Society Opens New Delhi Office for its Policy Institute |url=https://www.southasiatimes.com.au/australia/asia-society-opens-new-delhi-office-for-its-policy-institute/ |access-date=November 26, 2024 |work=South Asia Times |archive-date=December 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203085215/https://www.southasiatimes.com.au/australia/asia-society-opens-new-delhi-office-for-its-policy-institute/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Paris and Zurich). The Society's headquarters are in New York City, and includes a museum that exhibits pre-modern, modern, and contemporary art from Asia, Oceania and the Asian diaspora.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=November 26, 2024 |title=Asia Society Museum |url=https://www.sothebys.com/en/museums/asia-society-museum |access-date=November 26, 2024 |website=[[Sotheby's]] |archive-date=December 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203061735/https://www.sothebys.com/en/museums/asia-society-museum |url-status=live }}</ref> Asia Society also publishes an online magazine, ''ChinaFile''.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-03-11 |title=About |url=https://www.chinafile.com/about |access-date=2024-10-26 |website=ChinaFile |language=en |archive-date=October 21, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241021152955/https://www.chinafile.com/about |url-status=live }}</ref>

In January 2024, [[Kang Kyung-wha|Kyung-wha Kang]], who served as the first female Minister of Foreign Affairs of South Korea, from 2017 to 2021, was named its president and CEO, effective in April 2024;<ref name="Asia Society">{{Cite web |title=Asia Society names Dr. Kyung-wha Kang, South Korea's former Minister of Foreign Affairs, as President and CEO |url=https://asiasociety.org/asia-society-names-dr-kyung-wha-kang-south-koreas-former-minister-foreign-affairs-president-and-ceo |access-date=2024-01-24 |website=Asia Society |date=January 24, 2024 of the Asia Society as speaking on behalf of the United States in [[track II diplomacy]].<ref name=":2" />

==History==
[[File:Asia Society.svg|thumb|left|140px|Asia Society logo (1997–2021).]]
The Asia Society was founded in 1956 by [[John D. Rockefeller III|John D. Rockefeller 3rd]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About the Rockefellers |url=https://rockarch.org/resources/about-the-rockefellers/ |access-date=November 26, 2024 |website=Rockefeller Archive Center |archive-date=November 23, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241123021347/https://rockarch.org/resources/about-the-rockefellers/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.warnerbros.com/news/press-releases/asia-society-southern-california-announces-2018-us-china-entertainment-summit-gala |title= Asia Society Southern California Announces 2018 U.S.-China Entertainment Summit & Gala Dinner |work= [[Warner Bros.]] |date= October 4, 2018 |access-date= October 27, 2023 |archive-date= October 27, 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20231027071529/https://www.warnerbros.com/news/press-releases/asia-society-southern-california-announces-2018-us-china-entertainment-summit-gala |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="nytimes_com">{{Cite news |last=Glueck |first=Grace |date=1974-02-08 |title=John D. Rockefeller 3d Gives $10-Million in Art to Asia Society |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/02/08/archives/john-d-rockefeller-3d-gives-10million-in-art-to-asia-society-john-d.html |access-date=2024-05-25 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=May 25, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240525163929/https://www.nytimes.com/1974/02/08/archives/john-d-rockefeller-3d-gives-10million-in-art-to-asia-society-john-d.html |url-status=live |author-link=Grace Glueck}}</ref> In 1974, Rockefeller donated 300 objects of Asian art (worth between $10 and $15 million) to the Asia Society.<ref name="nytimes_com" />

The Asia Society's original focus was explaining aspects about Asia to Americans, and Robin Pogrebin of ''[[The New York Times]]'' said that it was "[l]ong regarded as a New York institution with regional branches".<ref name="2012 expansion" /> Around 2011, the society was refocusing efforts on augmenting partnerships amongst Asians and between Asians and Americans in business, culture, education, and public policy. In 2011, Pogrebin said "over the last few years [it] has aimed to recast itself as an international organization, partly through the construction of the two major centers in Houston<ref>{{Cite news |last= |date=April 5, 2012 |title=Asia Society Texas Center celebrates new building opening with First Look Festival |url=https://www.chron.com/life/health/article/Asia-Society-Texas-Center-celebrates-new-building-9367159.php |access-date=November 26, 2024 |work=[[Houston Chronicle]] |archive-date=December 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203041443/https://www.chron.com/life/health/article/Asia-Society-Texas-Center-celebrates-new-building-9367159.php |url-status=live }}</ref> and Hong Kong<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lau |first=Joyce |date=2012-02-22 |title=Asia Society Opens in Hong Kong |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/23/arts/23iht-asiasociety23.html |access-date=2026-09-09 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=December 4, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204000648/https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/23/arts/23iht-asiasociety23.html |url-status=live }}</ref> where it previously had only offices".<ref name="2012 expansion" /> The organization's records are held at the [[Rockefeller Archive Center]] in [[Sleepy Hollow, New York]].<ref name="HudsonIndependent">{{Cite web|url=https://thehudsonindependent.com/treasures-within-a-treasure-the-rockefeller-archives-center/|title=Treasures Within a Treasure: The Rockefeller Archives Center|website=thehudsonindependent.com|last=Seaman|first=Barrett|date=February 27, 2018|language=en-US|access-date=January 4, 2019|archive-date=January 5, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190105042958/https://thehudsonindependent.com/treasures-within-a-treasure-the-rockefeller-archives-center/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Buildings==
===Headquarters===
The Society's Manhattan headquarters, at [[Park Avenue]] and East 70th Street on the [[Upper East Side]], is a nine-story building faced in smooth red [[Oklahoma]] granite designed by [[Edward Larrabee Barnes]] / John M.Y. Lee Architects<ref>{{Cite book|last=Barnes|first=Edward Larrabee|title=Edward Larrabee Barnes: Architect|publisher=Rizzoli International Publications|year=1995|isbn=978-0-8478-1821-1|location=New York, New York}}</ref> in 1980. Barnes gave the building a strong facade to continue the line along Park, and set it back from East 70th with a terraced garden buffering it between the street and the older houses on that block. The semicircular window on the upper story and variations in the color and finish of the granite are intended to evoke Asian cultures.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} [[Paul Goldberger]], architecture critic at ''[[The New York Times]]'', called it "an ambitious building, full of civilized intentions, some of which succeed and others that do not". In the former category he put the interiors and the overall shape; in the latter he included the facade.<ref name="Goldberger review of building">{{cite news|last=Goldberger|first=Paul|author-link=Paul Goldberger|title=Architecture: Asia Society Building, A Design Full of Civilized Intentions|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/11/arts/architecture-asia-society-building-a-design-full-of-civilized.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 11, 1981|access-date=October 30, 2010|archive-date=November 11, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121111151327/http://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/11/arts/architecture-asia-society-building-a-design-full-of-civilized.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1999, it was closed for 18 months so that new interiors, designed by [[Bartholomew Voorsanger]], could be built. During that time the society used the former [[Christie's]] Manhattan offices on [[59th Street (Manhattan)|59th Street]] as a temporary home. The completed renovation included a {{convert|24|ft|m|adj=mid|-high}} [[atrium (architecture)|atrium]] and cafe. The expansion doubled the museum's exhibition space, allowing the society space for special exhibitions in addition to displaying the Rockefeller Asian art collection on display.<ref name="2000s expansion">{{cite news|last=Vogel|first=Carol|title=Inside Art: Asia in Midtown|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/12/10/arts/inside-art.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=December 10, 1999|access-date=October 30, 2010|archive-date=April 6, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120406013014/http://www.nytimes.com/1999/12/10/arts/inside-art.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Robin Pogrebin]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' said in 2011 that the Asia Society is "perhaps best known for the elegance of its headquarters and galleries on Park Avenue at 70th Street".<ref name="2012 expansion" />

===Global expansion===

==== Asia Society Hong Kong Center ====
[[File:Asia Society Hong Kong Center Entrance 2021.jpg|thumb|Asia Society Hong Kong Center]]
2012 marked a major expansion, with the opening of multimillion-dollar buildings in Hong Kong and Houston, Texas.<ref name="2012 expansion">{{Cite news |last=Pogrebin |first=Robin |author-link=Robin Pogrebin |date=2012-02-01 |title=Asia Society Expands, East and West |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/02/arts/asia-society-expands-in-houston-and-hong-kong.html |access-date=2026-09-09 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=April 29, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120429113936/http://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/02/arts/asia-society-expands-in-houston-and-hong-kong.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Asia Society Hong Kong Centre|Hong Kong complex]], dedicated on February 9, 2012, is situated on the site of a former British military explosives magazine overlooking [[Victoria Harbour]] and includes numerous restored military buildings. The project was designed by architects [[Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects|Tod Williams and Billie Tsien]]. The Asia Society Hong Kong Center was established in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Asia Society Hong Kong Center |url=https://twbta.com/work/international/asia-society-hong-kong-center/ |access-date=November 26, 2024 |website=Tod Williams Billie Tsien, Architects |archive-date=November 27, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241127172631/https://twbta.com/work/international/asia-society-hong-kong-center/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Asia Society Texas Center in Houston====
[[File:AsiaSocietyHouston.JPG|thumb|Asia Society Texas Center in [[Houston]]]]
The Texas Center first opened in 1979. The current {{convert|40000|sqft|sqm|adj=on}} building, located in the [[Houston Museum District|city's museum district]], opened on May 6, 2012, and was designed by architect [[Yoshio Taniguchi]]. With a cost of $50 million, the Texas Center has a [[modernism|modernist]] style and was built with German-origin [[Jura Mountains|Jura]] [[limestone]] personally inspected by Taniguchi and his employees. The building includes glass walls, steam generated from the roofline, and a garden as significant elements.<ref>Luks and Rougeau, p. 44.</ref>

==== Asia Society Northern California ====
The Northern California Center was established in 1998 in the [[San Francisco Bay Area]].<ref name="ASNCAbout">{{cite web |title=Asia Society Northern California |url=https://asiasociety.org/northern-california/about/asia-society |publisher=Asia Society Northern California |date=24 March 2020 |access-date=14 August 2025 |archive-date=June 25, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250625164542/https://asiasociety.org/northern-california/about/asia-society |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{main|Asia Society Northern California}}

=== New York Museum ===
At its 70th Street headquarters, The Asia Society Museum is host to traditional, modern and contemporary exhibitions, film screenings, literary events and performances. The holdings include works  that date from the eleventh century BCE to the nineteenth century CE and include Chinese ceramics of the Song and Ming periods as well as works by contemporary Asian and Asian diaspora artists.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} The museum's collection of traditional objects stems from a donation from Asia Society founder John D. Rockefeller 3rd and Blanchette Ferry Hooker Rockefeller, who contributed a number of items in 1978.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Asia Society Museum Highlights |url=https://museum.asiasociety.org/collection |access-date=November 26, 2024 |website=Asia Society Museum |archive-date=November 27, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241127174155/https://museum.asiasociety.org/collection |url-status=live }}</ref> The society began actively collecting contemporary Asian art with a 2007 initiative.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pogrebin |first=Robin |author-link=Robin Pogrebin |date=September 5, 2007 |title=Asia Society Will Build a Contemporary Art Collection |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/09/05/arts/design/05asia.html |access-date=October 17, 2016 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=September 22, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150922201004/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/09/05/arts/design/05asia.html |url-status=live}}</ref> A major renovation was completed in 2001, doubling the size of the four public galleries and expanding space for educational programming and including conference spaces and an auditorium.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.voorsanger.com/recent_projects/11|title=Asia Society & Museum|website=Voorsanger Architects PC|access-date=October 17, 2016|archive-date=October 9, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009080347/http://www.voorsanger.com/recent_projects/11|url-status=live}}</ref>

The headquarters also houses a museum shop and café. Forbes has listed the Garden Court Cafe (now the Leo Café<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leo Cafe |url=https://asiasociety.org/new-york/leo-cafe |access-date=November 26, 2024 |website=Asia Society |date=February 9, 2024 |archive-date=December 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203052522/https://asiasociety.org/new-york/leo-cafe |url-status=live }}</ref>) on its All-Star Eateries in New York list several times.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.forbes.com/forbes/2008/1222/019c.html|title=The Forbes 2008 All-Star Eateries in New York: Special|last=Forbes|first=Steve|date=December 4, 2008|work=Forbes|access-date=October 17, 2016|archive-date=August 2, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160802085858/http://www.forbes.com/forbes/2008/1222/019c.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Functions==

===Business===
From 1998 to 2010, the Asia Society annually presented a Corporate Conference in Asia, which functioned as a fundraiser, to examine the implications of macroeconomic trends and geopolitical developments for the region and the world.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Restructuring Industries and Corporate Governance |url=https://ciaotest.cc.columbia.edu/conf/ass10/ayj01.html |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=ciaotest.cc.columbia.edu}}</ref> Heads of Asian governments were often featured, as well as roundtable discussions with business and policy leaders from around the world.<ref name="Corporate Conferences">[http://asiasociety.org/business-economics/corporate-conferences] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090719091008/http://asiasociety.org/business-economics/corporate-conferences|date=July 19, 2009}}</ref>

===Education===
The Asia Society's Education department has two primary objectives: one focusing on teaching and learning about Asia in the United States and the other on the expansion of US investments in international studies at the elementary and secondary school levels.<ref name="2000s expansion"/>

===Policy===
The Asia Society houses two policy institutions. The Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), founded in 2014,<ref>{{Cite news |last=He |first=Amy |date=April 9, 2024 |title=Asia Society in NYC launches think tank |url=https://usa.chinadaily.com.cn/world/2014-04/09/content_17418467.htm |access-date=November 26, 2024 |work=[[China Daily]] |archive-date=December 1, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241201075402/https://usa.chinadaily.com.cn/world/2014-04/09/content_17418467.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> is a think tank that works with policy-makers and experts in Asia.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) {{!}} Devex |url=https://www.devex.com/organizations/asia-society-policy-institute-aspi-111205 |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=www.devex.com |archive-date=May 25, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240525171155/https://www.devex.com/organizations/asia-society-policy-institute-aspi-111205 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The Center on U.S.-China Relations was established in 2006 with a gift from [[Arthur Ross (philanthropist)|Arthur Ross]] with the goal of helping to forge a more constructive bilateral relationship. The Center undertakes projects and events which explore areas of common interest and divergent views between the two countries, focusing on policy, culture, business, media, economics, energy and the environment.{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}} [[Orville Schell]] is the current director of the center.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pogrebin |first=Robin |author-link=Robin Pogrebin |date=2006-09-26 |title=Journalist and China Expert to Head Center at Asia Society |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/09/26/arts/journalist-and-china-expert-to-head-center-at-asia-society.html |access-date=2026-09-09 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=December 4, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204035548/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/09/26/arts/journalist-and-china-expert-to-head-center-at-asia-society.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Orville Schell, Arthur Ross Director |url=https://asiasociety.org/center-us-china-relations/orville-schell-arthur-ross-director |access-date=November 26, 2024 |website=Asia Society Center on U.S.-China Relations |date=July 24, 2017 |archive-date=December 2, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241202223050/https://asiasociety.org/center-us-china-relations/orville-schell-arthur-ross-director |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2018 the Center on U.S.-China Relations co-produced a report with the [[Hoover Institution]], ''Chinese Influence & American Interests: Promoting Constructive Vigilance'', which examined Chinese influence efforts across American institutions and called for what its authors termed constructive vigilance. The report was the subject of a panel discussion at [[Stanford University]] in February 2019.<ref name="StanfordAPARC2019">{{cite web |title=Chinese Influence: Real or Perceived? |url=https://aparc.fsi.stanford.edu/china/multimedia/transcripts-chinese-influence-real-or-perceived |website=Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center |publisher=Stanford University |date=February 11, 2019 |access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref>

===Partnerships===
In May 2020, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], the Asia Society partnered with the nonprofit organization East Coast Coalition for Tolerance and Non-Discrimination and the [[Rockefeller Foundation]] to host a virtual forum entitled ''Standing Against Racism in the Time of COVID.''<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-04-17 |title=Standing Against Racism in the Time of COVID-19 |url=https://www.apha.org/events-and-meetings/apha-calendar/webinar-events/2020/standing-against-racism |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417071305/https://www.apha.org/events-and-meetings/apha-calendar/webinar-events/2020/standing-against-racism |archive-date=2021-04-17  |access-date=2022-07-21 |website=American Public Health Association}}</ref> Speakers at the forum included Representative [[Ted Lieu]], then-Los Angeles Mayor [[Eric Garcetti]], community organizer Bincheng Mao, and actor [[Tzi Ma]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Webinar: Standing Against Racism in the Time of COVID |url=https://china.usc.edu/calendar/webinar-standing-against-racism-time-covid |access-date=2022-07-21 |website=USC |language=en |archive-date=July 7, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220707103032/https://china.usc.edu/calendar/webinar-standing-against-racism-time-covid |url-status=live}}</ref> The Asia Society maintains a strategic partnership with the [[Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Partners |url=https://asiasociety.org/us-china-dialogue/partners |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929010616/http://asiasociety.org/us-china-dialogue/partners |archive-date=2017-09-29 |access-date=2020-09-19 |website=Asia Society |language=en}}</ref>

== Controversy ==

===Blocking pro-democracy activist from attending event===
Pro-democracy activist and secretary-general of [[Demosistō|Demosisto]] [[Joshua Wong (activist)|Joshua Wong]] was allegedly disallowed by Asia Society Hong Kong from speaking at a book launch originally scheduled to take place at its Hong Kong venue on June 28, 2017. Asia Society Hong Kong was approached by PEN Hong Kong to co-curate the book launch, but negotiations stalled upon the former's request for a more diverse panel of speakers. [[PEN Hong Kong]], a nonprofit organization supporting literature and freedom of expression, eventually decided to relocate the launch of ''Hong Kong 20/20: Reflections on a Borrowed Place'' – of which Wong was one of the authors – to the [[Foreign Correspondents' Club, Hong Kong|Foreign Correspondents Club]]. Joshua Wong said that Asia Society Hong Kong needs to give a "reasonable explanation" for the incident.<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last=Tong |first=Elson |date=July 6, 2017 |title=Asia Society faces backlash as Joshua Wong demands explanation over 'blocked' book launch |url=https://www.hongkongfp.com/2017/07/06/asia-society-faces-backlash-joshua-wong-demands-explanation-blocked-book-launch/ |access-date=July 6, 2017 |website=[[Hong Kong Free Press]] |archive-date=October 21, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231021190452/https://hongkongfp.com/2017/07/06/asia-society-faces-backlash-joshua-wong-demands-explanation-blocked-book-launch/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

"The mission of PEN Hong Kong is to promote literature and defend the freedom of expression. To bar one of the contributors to our anthology, whether it is Joshua Wong or somebody else, from speaking at our launch event would undermine and in fact contravene that mission," said PEN Hong Kong President Jason Y. Ng.<ref name=":0" />

Back to November 2016, Asia Society Hong Kong also canceled a scheduled screening of Raise The Umbrellas, a documentary on the 2014 Occupy protests with appearance of Joshua Wong.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tatlow |first=Didi Kirsten |date=November 10, 2016 |title=Hong Kong Venue Cancels Screening of Protest Film, Citing Political Concerns |language=en-US |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/11/11/world/asia/hong-kong-umbrella-revolution-film.html |access-date=July 6, 2017 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=October 1, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171001213306/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/11/11/world/asia/hong-kong-umbrella-revolution-film.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Asia Society Hong Kong has similarly cited the lack of balanced speaker representation at the pre-screening talk as the reason for not screening the film.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

US Congressman [[Chris Smith (New Jersey politician)|Chris Smith]], co-chairperson of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China, expressed that "The Asia Society has some explaining to do after two events that featured Joshua Wong prominently were canceled over the past nine months," said the New Jersey representative. "I commend PEN Hong Kong for not appeasing the Asia Society's demands."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.facebook.com/PENHongKong/photos/a.1129327497162234.1073741828.1129137233847927/1456482501113397/?type=3&theater |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/iarchive/facebook/1129137233847927/1456482501113397 |archive-date=2022-02-26 |url-access=limited|title=PEN Hong Kong|website=www.facebook.com|language=en|access-date=July 6, 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

On July 7, 2017, Asia Society Hong Kong released a statement attributing the decision to an error in judgment at staff level. Asia Society Hong Kong emphasized they received no representations from the Chinese government on this matter, and Joshua Wong and speakers from all sides of the issue were welcome at Asia Society.<ref>{{Cite web|date=July 7, 2017|url=http://asiasociety.org/hong-kong/statement-pen-hong-kong-event#CRsAhwuS3Islo3B4.01|title=Statement on PEN Hong Kong Event|website=www.asiasociety.org|language=en|access-date=July 8, 2017|archive-date=July 15, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170715083743/http://asiasociety.org/hong-kong/statement-pen-hong-kong-event#CRsAhwuS3Islo3B4.01|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Ramzy |first=Austin |date=2017-07-07 |title=Asia Society Blames Staff for Barring Hong Kong Activist’s Speech |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/07/world/asia/hong-kong-joshua-wong-censorship.html |access-date=2026-09-09 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=November 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231107225325/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/07/world/asia/hong-kong-joshua-wong-censorship.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Haas |first=Benjamin |date=2017-07-06 |title=US-based Asia Society accused of kowtowing to China over Hong Kong activist |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/jul/06/asia-society-china-hong-kong-activist-joshua-wong |access-date=2026-09-09 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077 |archive-date=November 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231107225315/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/jul/06/asia-society-china-hong-kong-activist-joshua-wong |url-status=live }}</ref>

On July 10, 2017, Forbes magazine ran an article revealing Hong Kong real estate magnate and Asia Society Co-chair Ronnie Chan (a US citizen) to be the political force behind the Joshua Wong incident. It alleged that wealthy Asians have been behind US think tanks and NGOs and effectively turning them into foreign policy tools of the People's Republic of China (Beijing). However, the link to the article went dead a day later. It has been rumored that Asia Society or Ronnie Chan could be taking legal action against Forbes for libel.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.intellasia.net/chinese-influence-at-the-asia-society-elitism-and-radicalisation-in-hk-607591 |title= Chinese Influence At The Asia Society: Elitism And Radicalisation In HK |author= Forbes  |website= Intellasia |date= July 11, 2017 |access-date= January 28, 2021 |archive-date= January 28, 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210128075731/https://www.intellasia.net/chinese-influence-at-the-asia-society-elitism-and-radicalisation-in-hk-607591 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

On July 20, 2017, Asia Society Chairman Ronnie Chan defended the Hong Kong center's apolitical stance at an event in New York.  He reiterated the Hong Kong center's deliberate stance to stay away from local politics and to cover business and policy, education, arts and culture as an institution.  "At Asia Society, we generate not heat but light," he said.<ref>{{cite web|date=July 13, 2017|url=https://asiasociety.org/video/hong-kong-20-years-later-promises-made-promises-kept-promises-be-fulfilled-complete|title=Hong Kong, 20 Years Later: Promises Made, Promises Kept, Promises To Be Fulfilled|website=Asia Society|access-date=January 13, 2019|archive-date=January 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190114044401/https://asiasociety.org/video/hong-kong-20-years-later-promises-made-promises-kept-promises-be-fulfilled-complete|url-status=live}}</ref>

On August 4, 2017, Hong Kong international affairs commentator and newspaper columnist Simon Shen wrote in support of Asia Society Hong Kong's apolitical stance and described it as a "firewall" between international relations and local politics.  He pointed to the increasingly blinkered outlook of the local political discourse and argued for the need served by Asia Society to bring a broader perspective for understanding the role of Hong Kong in a global context.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ir-basilica.com/國際關係與本土政治的防火牆：由亞洲協會談起/ |title=國際關係與本土政治的防火牆：由亞洲協會談起 • 沈旭暉國際評論 |website=www.ir-basilica.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808153648/http://www.ir-basilica.com/%E5%9C%8B%E9%9A%9B%E9%97%9C%E4%BF%82%E8%88%87%E6%9C%AC%E5%9C%9F%E6%94%BF%E6%B2%BB%E7%9A%84%E9%98%B2%E7%81%AB%E7%89%86%EF%BC%9A%E7%94%B1%E4%BA%9E%E6%B4%B2%E5%8D%94%E6%9C%83%E8%AB%87%E8%B5%B7/ |archive-date=2017-08-08}}</ref>
